nodes.label: Definition
nodes.statement: A volume or logical drive is a distinctly-addressable storage area with a single file system.

nodes.label: Storage topology
nodes.statement: Mass storage is commonly divided into partitions used as volumes; volumes may span multiple media for redundancy, while simple volumes use one medium without redundancy or striping.

nodes.label: Windows example
nodes.statement: The source's two-drive example maps D0/P0 to NTFS C:, D0/P1 to FAT32 D:, and D1/P0 to FAT32 E:.

nodes.label: Partition versus volume recognition
nodes.statement: An OS may recognize a partition without recognizing its volume when it is unformatted or uses an unsupported filesystem such as ext4 in the Windows example.

nodes.label: File-packed volume
nodes.statement: A volume can be packed in one file, such as an ISO9660 disc image or Apple Disk Image; because it is a file inside a host volume, it is not a partition.

nodes.label: Windows mounting
nodes.statement: Windows handles volumes in the kernel and configures volumes/mount points through Disk Management or diskpart; mounted volumes receive paths via drive letters or NTFS mount points.

nodes.label: Unix mounting
nodes.statement: Unix-like systems commonly use volume managers and mount; non-boot volumes are grafted into the filesystem tree at a mount point.

nodes.label: Cross-volume performance
nodes.statement: Moving a file within a volume can change metadata without copying content, while moving across volumes requires copying content and deleting the source.

nodes.label: Identifiers
nodes.statement: Volumes can use human-readable labels and more fixed identifiers; serial numbers historically originated on mainframes and later supported media-change detection.

nodes.label: FAT/NTFS labels and serials
nodes.statement: FAT, NTFS, and exFAT impose different volume-label constraints; FAT/NTFS serial numbers support detection of volume replacement and formatting changes the serial.

nodes.author: Brett Glass

nodes.label: Origin of volume serial numbers
nodes.description: Volume serial numbers originated with mainframes in the 1950s.

nodes.label: OS/2 development context
nodes.description: The FAT/NTFS identification system was designed during OS/2 development.

nodes.label: MS-DOS 4.01 introduction
nodes.description: The source says the volume serial number mechanism was introduced in MS-DOS 4.01 in 1988.

nodes.label: Partition Vs Volume
nodes.distinction: A partition is a storage division; a volume is the logically addressable storage area with a filesystem.

nodes.label: Volume Vs Physical Drive
nodes.distinction: A volume is logical; a physical drive is physical storage hardware.

nodes.label: Simple Vs Redundant
nodes.distinction: Simple volumes use one medium without redundancy or striping; specialized volumes may span media.

nodes.label: Volume File Vs Partition
nodes.distinction: A volume packed into a file is stored as a file inside a host volume and is not itself a partition.

nodes.label: Drive Letter Vs Mount Point
nodes.distinction: Windows can identify a volume by a drive letter or mount it at a path within an NTFS volume.

nodes.label: Windows Vs Unix Mount
nodes.distinction: Windows uses drive letters and NTFS mount points; Unix-like systems graft volumes into one filesystem tree.

nodes.label: Same Vs Cross Volume Move
nodes.distinction: Same-volume moves can alter metadata; cross-volume moves require data copying.

nodes.label: Label Vs Serial
nodes.distinction: Labels are user-assignable; serial numbers are generally fixed and less human-readable.

nodes.label: Format Vs Relabel
nodes.distinction: Formatting typically changes serial number; relabeling does not.

nodes.label: Filesystem Support
nodes.distinction: Recognizing a partition does not guarantee recognition of its volume filesystem.

nodes.label: Iso Volume Vs Partition
nodes.distinction: An ISO9660 disc image can represent a volume in a file rather than a partition.

nodes.label: Logical Vs Global Id
nodes.distinction: Human-readable identifiers differ from fixed/global identifiers.

nodes.label: Volume identity model
nodes.expression: Volume = distinctly-addressable storage area + single filesystem

nodes.label: Simple volume
nodes.expression: volume = one storage medium + no redundancy + no striping

nodes.label: Windows volume path
nodes.expression: volume -> drive letter OR NTFS mount point -> file path

nodes.label: Unix mount model
nodes.expression: volume filesystem tree -> graft at existing mount-point directory

nodes.label: Same-volume move
nodes.expression: same volume + move -> metadata change; content need not copy

nodes.label: Cross-volume move
nodes.expression: different volumes + move -> copy content + delete source

nodes.label: Volume identification
nodes.expression: volume -> human label + fixed serial/global identifier

nodes.label: Media-change detection
nodes.expression: current volume serial != previous serial -> possible volume exchange

nodes.label: File-packed volume
nodes.expression: volume image -> ordinary file in host volume; not partition

nodes.label: Storage performance
nodes.sequence: same-volume move -> metadata_change vs cross-volume move -> content_copy

nodes.label: Filesystem compatibility
nodes.sequence: partition -> unsupported filesystem -> volume not recognized

nodes.label: A volume is always a physical disk.
nodes.correction: A volume is logical and may be partition-based, span media, or be packed in a file.

nodes.label: Every partition is automatically a usable volume.
nodes.correction: An OS can recognize a partition without recognizing its volume filesystem.

nodes.label: An ISO volume is a partition.
nodes.correction: The source treats an ISO9660 volume image as a file in a host volume, not a partition.

nodes.label: Windows and Unix-like systems expose volumes the same way.
nodes.correction: Windows uses drive letters/NTFS mount points; Unix-like systems graft volumes into a filesystem tree.

nodes.label: Moving a file always copies its data.
nodes.correction: Within one volume the move can be metadata-only; across volumes content must be copied.

nodes.label: A volume label is a permanent unique identifier.
nodes.correction: Labels are user-assignable; serial numbers provide a more fixed identifier.

nodes.label: Relabeling and formatting have the same identity effect.
nodes.correction: Formatting typically changes the serial; relabeling does not.

nodes.label: A volume has exactly one path.
nodes.correction: The source allows multiple path forms, including multiple drive letters via SUBST.

nodes.label: A drive letter identifies physical hardware directly.
nodes.correction: A drive letter identifies a logical volume in the OS namespace.

nodes.label: FAT, NTFS and exFAT use identical label constraints.
nodes.correction: The source gives different limits and character behavior for each.
